clue.text: Varsity type is able to hit back

parts.note: is able means can

indicators.note: back tells us the word for hit is read from right to left

parts.note: to hit is to bat, as with a cricket bat

explanation.surface: A university student who can hit back, perhaps on the cricket field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Varsity' is the British word for the Oxford and Cambridge universities; 'back' turns the word for hit round.
explanation.definitionFit: Cantab is the short form of Cantabrigian, a member of Cambridge University, so a varsity type.

clue.text: Order from the menu

parts.note: a dessert you might order in a restaurant, and also the phrase for perfect neatness

explanation.surface: Choosing a dish from a restaurant menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apple-pie order' means perfect tidiness, and an apple pie is something you might order from the menu.
explanation.definitionFit: The dessert is a menu item, and the phrase 'in apple-pie order' means neat and orderly.

clue.text: He doesn't take a one sided view of dress

definitions.text: He doesn't take a one sided view of dress

parts.words: He doesn't take a one sided view of dress
parts.note: a jacket worn inside out shows its other side, just as a renegade switches loyalty

explanation.surface: A man who sees clothing from more than one angle.
explanation.walkthrough: A deserter of a party or cause was said to wear his coat inside out, showing its other side.
explanation.definitionFit: A renegade who switches sides is said to have reversed his jacket.

clue.text: A room or its chairless occupant ?

explanation.surface: A small flat and the person who lives in it without furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: A bed-sitter is a British one-room flat; with no chair, its occupant must sit on the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A bed-sitter is a single combined bedroom and living room; someone without a chair is a 'bed sitter' by perching on the bed.

clue.text: A check for absentees, do we hear at the dice game ?

definitions.text: do we hear at the dice game

explanation.surface: A teacher's register is compared to the noise of a game of dice.
explanation.walkthrough: At dice you roll and the result is called out, so the second half reads as a 'roll call' of the throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Reading out names to see who is missing is the register-taking routine; at dice the throw is rolled and its score called.

clue.text: They should present no difficulty to the make-up expert

definitions.text: They should present no difficulty to the make-up expert

parts.words: They should present no difficulty to the make-up expert
parts.note: the expert is not a cosmetician but someone skilled at making up after quarrels

explanation.surface: Faces that a theatre's cosmetics artist should find easy to work on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make-up' suggests cosmetics, but 'make up' also means settle a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Ending a quarrel and becoming friends again is making up, so these come easily to one skilled at it.

clue.text: Measures of fever among the French

indicators.note: among puts the word for fever amid the letters of the French article

parts.note: les is French for 'the' (plural)
an ague is a fever with shivering, such as malaria

explanation.surface: Gauging the fevers suffered among French people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measures' looks like a verb with 'fever' as its object, but it is the plural noun defining old distance units.
explanation.definitionFit: A league is an old unit of distance, about three miles.

clue.text: Leicester Square bade farewell to Granada's Palace

explanation.surface: A London square says goodbye to a Spanish palace.
explanation.walkthrough: The Alhambra Theatre in London's Leicester Square was demolished in 1936; the Alhambra is the Moorish palace-fortress at Granada in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous London music hall that closed shared its name with the Moorish palace at Granada.

clue.text: Medal one madly thirsts for?

indicators.note: madly says the letters of the two words are scrambled wildly

explanation.surface: An athlete desperately craving a medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' rearranges MEDAL and ONE; the whole clue then describes the drink one thirsts for.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold citrus drink is what a thirsty person craves.

clue.text: Cops raid madly scattered

indicators.note: madly says the letters of the two words are thrown into wild disorder

explanation.surface: Police raid a place wildly and send people scattering.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sporadic happens here and there, irregularly, as if scattered.

clue.text: A measure to comprehend

explanation.surface: A unit of measurement and a verb for understanding.
explanation.definitionFit: A fathom is a six-foot depth unit used at sea; to fathom something is to understand it.

clue.text: What one might expect from sappers in war-time ?

parts.note: sappers are army engineers, the Royal Engineers, abbreviated RE
soldiers in war-time are in action

explanation.surface: Asking what military engineers would be expected to do during a war.
explanation.walkthrough: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, the British Army corps whose soldiers are called sappers.
explanation.definitionFit: A reaction is the response one expects to follow an action.

clue.text: They don't wander aimlessly

parts.note: people who carry pistols do not act without aim: they literally point weapons

explanation.surface: Purposeful people who never drift about without a goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aimlessly' means without purpose, but here it is read literally: these men always take aim.
explanation.definitionFit: Armed criminals take aim with their firearms, so they are never 'aimless'.

clue.text: Instances of rising production by workers

definitions.text: Instances of rising production by workers

parts.words: Instances of rising production by workers
parts.note: the workers are insects of the colony, and what they produce rises up as mounds

explanation.surface: Examples of increasing industrial output by a workforce.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords 'workers' often means ants; their 'rising production' is a heap of earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Ants build mounds of earth that rise from the ground, the product of their labour.

clue.text: Moral state of fast women, oddly enough

definitions.text: Moral state of fast women, oddly enough

parts.words: Moral state of fast women, oddly enough
parts.note: fast women are loose in morals, yet fast normally means firmly fixed, the opposite of loose

explanation.surface: Commentary on the morals of racy women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' can mean firmly fixed, the opposite of slack, so describing fast women as slack is odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Laxity of morals is the slack state associated with 'fast' women, though fast also means tightly fixed.

clue.text: The loquacious are rudely requested to do this up

definitions.text: The loquacious are rudely requested to do this up

parts.words: The loquacious are rudely requested to do this up
parts.note: talkative people are told impolitely to be quiet with a phrase that also means fastening a strap

explanation.surface: Chatterboxes are told, not politely, to tighten something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belt up!' is British slang for 'shut up', while doing up a belt is fastening it.
explanation.definitionFit: A strap round the waist is done up, and 'belt up' is a rude order to stop talking.

clue.text: It pays them to start a new life

definitions.text: It pays them to start a new life

parts.words: It pays them to start a new life
parts.note: not emigrants making a fresh start, but people who profit by producing offspring of animals

explanation.surface: People rewarded for making a fresh start somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start a new life' suggests emigration; literally it is bringing new animals into being.
explanation.definitionFit: People who raise livestock profit from producing young animals.

clue.text: A man of action

parts.note: the action is a lawsuit, so this person is involved in legal proceedings

explanation.surface: A dynamic, energetic man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'action' here is a legal action, a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A party to a lawsuit is involved in a legal action.

clue.text: A strip of gutta-percha

indicators.note: of says the strip is taken out from within the letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A piece of the rubbery material gutta-percha.
explanation.walkthrough: The four letters run across the hyphen of 'gutta-percha'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tape is a long narrow band of material, a strip.

clue.text: Make-up artist as a member of a Royal house

definitions.text: a member of a Royal house

indicators.note: make up means compose afresh, so the letters are put together in a new order

explanation.surface: A make-up artist working for royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up' rearranges ARTIST and AS.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsaritsa was the wife of a Russian tsar, a member of the imperial family.

clue.text: Fleet street's answer to the Pullman?

definitions.text: Fleet street's answer to the Pullman?

parts.words: Fleet street's answer to the Pullman?
parts.note: a Pullman is a luxury railway car; the newspaper world's equivalent swaps pull for its own verb

explanation.surface: Newspapers' rival to the luxury railway carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street was London's newspaper district; a Pullman is a luxury railway carriage, read as 'pull man'.
explanation.definitionFit: A journalist works for the newspaper press, as a 'pull man' would pull.

clue.text: Anything but country lovers?

parts.note: not lovers of the countryside but people who are the very opposite of patriots

explanation.surface: People who are anything but fans of rural life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'country lovers' suggests rural enthusiasts; it means patriots, who love their nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who betray their nation are the opposite of patriots.

clue.text: Used by painter of a beautiful vale ?

definitions.text: Used by painter of a beautiful vale

parts.note: the Vale of Tempe in Greece was famed for its beauty
RA, Royal Academician, is a painter

explanation.surface: A landscape artist's material for depicting a lovely valley.
explanation.walkthrough: TEMPE is the Greek vale celebrated by poets; RA is a member of the Royal Academy. The whole clue also says what such a painter uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg-based paint is a medium used by artists.

clue.text: A gem in wrong setting can be a bit of a problem

indicators.note: putting the letters in the wrong setting means rearranging them

explanation.surface: A jewel placed in the wrong mount is something of a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong setting' rearranges A, GEM and IN.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is a puzzle or mystery, something of a problem.

clue.text: One who may be practically useless ?

definitions.text: One who may be practically useless

parts.words: One who may be practically useless
parts.note: 'practically' means in practice rather than almost: someone strong on ideas but weak in practice

explanation.surface: Someone who is almost entirely useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'practically useless' reads as 'nearly useless' but means useless at the practical side.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who deals in ideas and hypotheses may be poor at practical work.

clue.text: One way to get a shiny face

definitions.text: One way to get a shiny face

parts.words: One way to get a shiny face
parts.note: not a person's face but a surface, such as a clock dial or a coated pot, given a glossy finish

explanation.surface: Advice on how to make one's face gleam.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'face' is a surface, such as a dial or pot, given a glossy coat.
explanation.definitionFit: A glassy coating fired onto metal or pottery gives a glossy surface.

clue.text: But it's not beyond the bowler's normal stint

definitions.text: But it's not beyond the bowler's normal stint

parts.words: But it's not beyond the bowler's normal stint
parts.note: extra hours worked are beyond normal time, but the first part of the word is a cricket bowler's standard spell of six balls

explanation.surface: A remark about what a cricket bowler is normally expected to bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: Hours worked beyond normal time; yet its first part, OVER, is a cricket bowler's standard stint of six balls, which is not 'beyond' anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtime is work done beyond normal hours, while an over is the regular unit a cricket bowler bowls.

clue.text: Place sporting defenders when you have reverses

parts.note: to place is to set
in football and rugby defenders are called backs

explanation.surface: A coach positioning defenders after the team has suffered defeats.
explanation.definitionFit: Setbacks are reverses, checks to progress.

clue.text: Lovers often seen on a boat

definitions.text: Lovers often seen on a boat

parts.words: Lovers often seen on a boat
parts.note: the word for rustic suitors often appears after the word boat, forming a ship's officer

explanation.surface: Courting couples commonly spotted on a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Put 'boat' on the front and you get BOATSWAINS, ship's officers often seen aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Swains are young suitors or rustic lovers, and a boatswain is a ship's petty officer.
